summary: This investigative piece surveys marriage customs and love legends from Scotland, Japan, China, France, Nepal, Ghana and India, pairing each ritual with its origin story and an expert's comment. It shows how traditions such as handfasting, San San Kudo, the Pote, and Jaimala carry symbolism of unity, commitment and blessing. The article concludes that a universal human desire for blessing, solidarity and harmony underlies diverse wedding practices.
one_line: A global tour of wedding rituals and love legends, from Scottish handfasting to Indian Jaimala, explaining their origins and symbolism.
key_facts: Handfasting, a Scottish ritual of binding hands, was performed in the Scottish Highlands on September 14, 2023, and dates to Celtic days when marriages were agreements of mutual benefit.
Margaret MacDonald of the University of Edinburgh says handfasting was essentially a trial marriage: couples bound hands for a year and a day before deciding to part or commit for life.
San San Kudo, the sharing of nuptial cups, was performed by Kenji and Sakura in Kyoto on October 22, 2023; the couple takes three sips from three sake cups.
San San Kudo traces to the Heian period, when sharing sake was a Shinto tradition marking formal bonds; Hiromi Tanaka says the three cups represent hatred, passion, and ignorance.
China's 'Butterfly Lovers' (Liang Zhu) legend tells of Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, forbidden to marry, who reincarnated as butterflies after death.
Couples mark the 'Qi Xi' anniversary, the Chinese equivalent of Valentine's Day, and often use butterfly decorations in weddings, says Beijing wedding planner Feng Mian.
France's 'Charivari' is a loud, raucous event held the night before a wedding, dating to the Middle Ages, in which villagers made noise outside the couple's home to ward off bad spirits.
Historian Luc Martel calls the Charivari 'part performance, part protest'; today it is a celebration of love and community inclusion.
On November 5, 2023, in Patan's Durbar Square, bride Anusha received the 'Pote', a necklace of green, yellow, and red glass beads, from groom Rajesh.
The Pote is worn only by married women and represents long life for the husband and the strength of the marital bond; bead colors and patterns vary by ethnic group, per Priya Bhattarai.
Ama and Kojo tied a knot binding their wrists with Kente cloth near Accra, Ghana, on December 12, 2023; folklorist Nana Abeka says the knot symbolizes strength, unity and commitment.
Seema and Sunil performed the 'Jaimala' garland exchange in Jaipur on January 17, 2024, mirroring the love of Lord Krishna and Radha, according to cultural expert Anil Mehta.
